blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Flash-Friendly File System (F2FS) from Samsung as a novel file system design optimized for NAND flash storage, addressing key limitations like erase-before-write requirements and sequential write constraints. He emphasizes F2FS's performance improvements (2-3x over EXT4) and its innovative features such as multi-head logging for hot/cold data separation, adaptive logging to mitigate fragmentation at high utilization, and roll-forward recovery for efficient fsync operations. The blog underscores the importance of tailoring file system designs to flash storage characteristics rather than relying on traditional HDD-oriented approaches.
paper_title: F2FS: A New File System for Flash Storage
paper_abstract: F2FS is a Linux file system designed to perform well on modern flash storage devices. The file system builds on append-only logging and its key design decisions were made with the characteristics of flash storage in mind. This paper describes the main design ideas, data structures, algorithms and the resulting performance of F2FS. Experimental results highlight the desirable performance of F2FS; on a state-of-the-art mobile system, it outperforms EXT4 under synthetic workloads by up to 3.1× (iozone) and 2× (SQLite). It reduces elapsed time of several realistic workloads by up to 40%. On a server system, F2FS is shown to perform better than EXT4 by up to 2.5× (SATA SSD) and 1.8× (PCIe SSD).
